sections.title: Ultrasonic and Infrasonic Waves, and their Applications

slides.title: How fast sound travels
slides.kicker: Chasing a crest across the room
bullets: The speed of sound describes how fast sound waves propagate through a medium.
In terms of compressions and rarefactions, think of speed as how fast these density disturbances travel through the medium.
Formally, speed is the distance which a point on a wave, such as a crest or a trough, travels in unit time.
slides.note: Crest ko race mein daalo, speed mil jaayegi!

slides.title: The wave speed formula
slides.kicker: One wavelength covered per time period
bullets: A disturbance covers exactly one wavelength, the gap between two consecutive crests, in one time period T.
So speed = wavelength / time period, which becomes speed = wavelength x frequency.
The book writes this as Equation 10.2: speed of sound = wavelength x frequency.

items: Covered in one time period T

slides.note: Equation 10.2 yaad rakho!

slides.title: Medium changes the speed
slides.kicker: Solids race, gases take it slow
bullets: The speed of sound depends on the medium: it travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases.
Sound travels about 4 to 5 times faster in water than in air.
In solids it is typically 15 to 20 times faster than in air.
slides.note: Particles jitne paas-paas, sound utni tez!

slides.title: Warm and humid means faster
slides.kicker: Weather nudges the speed of sound
bullets: The speed of sound in air also depends on the temperature and humidity.
As we increase the temperature or the humidity, the speed of sound increases.
In dry air the speed is about 331 m/s at 0 degrees C and nearly 344 m/s at 22 degrees C.
slides.note: Garmi badhi toh sound bhi bhaagega!

slides.title: Measured waves, felt sound
bullets: Time period, wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed are physical properties that are well-defined and can be measured.
How we experience sound is subjective, so we describe it using terms like loudness and pitch.
Loudness and pitch do not have simple relations with the physical properties of the wave.
slides.note: Same speaker, alag feel for everyone!

slides.title: Pitch is heard frequency
bullets: Pitch is how the frequency of a sound is perceived by humans.
Shrill sounds, such as a whistle or a siren, are said to have high pitch, so they generally have higher frequency.
Deep sounds like thunder or an aircraft rumble have low pitch and lower frequency.
The exact mathematical relation between pitch and frequency is complicated.

left.title: High pitch
items: Shrill, like a whistle or siren

right.title: Low pitch
items: Deep, like thunder or an aircraft rumble

slides.note: Whistle upar, thunder neeche!

slides.title: Why voices sound different
slides.kicker: Throat, mouth and nose shape you
bullets: Male, female and children's voices differ not just in frequency but also in how the sound is shaped by the throat, mouth and nasal cavities.
During adolescence, the vocal cords of boys lengthen and thicken and vibrate less frequently, thus deepening their voice.
slides.note: Teen voice change is pure physics!

slides.title: The audible range
slides.kicker: 20 Hz to 20 kHz, more or less
bullets: Humans can only hear a limited range of sound frequencies, called the audible range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
This range varies from person to person and decreases with age.
Sound below 20 Hz is called infrasonic; sound above 20 kHz is called ultrasonic.
Dogs, cats, bats and dolphins can detect ultrasound, while elephants can detect infrasound.
slides.note: Hum kuch nahi sunte, elephant sun leta hai!

slides.title: Loudness is felt amplitude
bullets: Humans perceive the amplitude of a sound wave as loudness.
Sounds with larger amplitude are heard louder, while those with smaller amplitude sound softer.
The loudness decreases as we move farther away from the source.
In everyday language, loudness and intensity are used interchangeably, but intensity is a measurable quantity.
slides.note: Door jaoge toh awaaz dhundhli!

slides.title: Sound bounces back
bullets: Sound waves can bounce off obstacles like solids or liquids; this is known as the reflection of sound.
One of the most common examples of the reflection of sound is an echo.
slides.note: Awaaz ki utpatan, simple bounce!

slides.title: Sound obeys light's laws
bullets: Sound follows the same laws of reflection as those of light.
The incident and reflected sound make equal angles with the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.
All three directions, incident, normal and reflected, lie in the same plane.

items: Normal is drawn at the point of incidence
Reflected sound leaves at an equal angle
All three directions stay in one plane

slides.note: Angle i equals angle r, sound ke liye bhi!

slides.title: From bounce to echo
bullets: Any hard obstacle, like a solid wall, can act as a reflecting surface for sound waves.
When the reflected sound reaches you after a noticeable gap, you hear it as an echo.
This simple bounce is the seed for echoes, reverberation and even sonar in the coming sections.
slides.note: Ek bounce se poora chapter banta hai!

slides.title: Hear your own shout
bullets: If we shout near a mountain, a cliff, or in a long corridor, we may hear our voice again after some time; this is an echo.
The sound reflects off the hard surface of a distant object and comes back to us.
slides.note: Pahaad tumhari awaaz lautata hai!

slides.title: The 0.1 second rule
bullets: Echoes are not heard everywhere; in a small room, wall reflections arrive too quickly for the brain to separate them.
If the time gap between two sounds reaching us is at least 0.1 s, we can hear them as separate sounds.
If the gap is less than 0.1 s, we cannot clearly distinguish between the two sounds.
slides.note: 0.1 second, brain ka secret password!

slides.title: Finding minimum echo distance
bullets: The 0.1 s gap helps us estimate the minimum distance of a reflecting surface from which an echo can be heard.
Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the distance covered in 0.1 s is 340 x 0.1 = 34.0 m.
Note that 34 m is the distance from the source to the surface and back.
Hence the minimum echo distance is half of this, that is 17 m.
slides.note: 17 m se paas ki deewar echo nahi degi!

slides.title: Surfaces make or break echoes
bullets: Echoes are stronger from hard and smooth surfaces that reflect sound.
Soft surfaces like curtains tend to absorb sound.
Rough surfaces scatter sound in different directions, so echoes cannot be heard clearly in such cases.

right.title: Weak or no echoes
items: Soft surfaces like curtains absorb sound

slides.note: Deewar sakht ho, echo mazboot!

slides.title: When sound refuses to stop
bullets: In a large hall or auditorium, the emitted sound can undergo multiple reflections from the walls.
Multiple reflections make sound persist after the source stops emitting it; this is called reverberation.
It occurs when sound reflections from surfaces arrive with a time difference less than 0.05 s.
slides.note: Gaana band, awaaz zinda!

slides.title: Designing halls for clear sound
bullets: Modern auditoriums and large concert halls are architecturally designed to have desirable reverberations.
Desirable reverberations let the audience everywhere hear speech, music and other sounds clearly without any distortions.
Too many reflections from unwanted sources could lead to garbled sound.
slides.note: Acoustics bhi ek art hai!

slides.title: Soft materials soak up sound
bullets: Sound absorbing panels, upholstered chairs, curtains and other soft, porous surfaces reduce reverberations.
These materials stop the unwanted reflections that would otherwise pile up into garbled sound.
slides.note: Naram cheezein awaaz nigal jaati hain!

slides.title: Gol Gumbaz whispers
slides.kicker: A dome that repeats your whisper
bullets: Medieval architects across the world, including in India, designed several monuments with deep acoustic insights.
The Whispering Gallery of the Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur, Karnataka, lets even a faint whisper be heard multiple times across the large dome.
slides.note: Ek whisper, kai dafa sunai de!

slides.title: Sound we cannot hear
bullets: Sound waves with frequencies outside the human audible range still exist all around us.
These waves have important applications in science, medicine and technology.
slides.note: Jo dikhta nahi, kaam aata hai!

slides.title: Infrasound keeps watch
bullets: Infrasonic waves are used for detecting natural events, such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
They are also used for detecting severe storms, as such waves travel long distances through air and the Earth.
slides.note: Prakriti ka warning system, infra style!

slides.title: Ultrasound at work
bullets: Ultrasonography uses ultrasound to image internal organs without surgery.
Ultrasound is used for breaking kidney stones into smaller pieces, which can then be passed out of the body.
Industries use it for ultrasonic welding and for cleaning delicate machine parts.
slides.note: Bina operation, organ ki tasveer!

slides.title: Ultrasound tests the metal
bullets: Ultrasonic waves are used for detecting defects inside metal blocks during construction and industrial testing.
They are also used for locating objects when sound waves get reflected off them.
slides.note: Metal ki chhupi hui kami pakdi jaati hai!

slides.title: Bats see with echoes
bullets: Bats are nocturnal creatures that fly and search for their prey in the dark without colliding into objects.
Most bats emit short bursts of ultrasonic waves which are reflected from nearby objects.
By sensing the echoes, the bat can determine the position of obstacles and prey.
slides.note: Andhera? Bats ka jawab hai echo!

slides.title: Echolocation, a shared skill
bullets: The ability to locate objects using reflected sound waves is called echolocation.
Besides bats, animals such as dolphins, whales and some birds also use echolocation for navigation and hunting.
slides.note: Sound se dekhna, poori jaanvar gang!

slides.title: Sonar goes underwater
bullets: Humans have adapted the same principle for underwater exploration through sonar, sound navigation and ranging.
In sonar, ultrasonic waves are sent into water and the reflected waves are analysed.
The reflections determine the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects, such as submarines or shipwrecks.

items: Sonar sends ultrasonic waves into water
Waves reflect off submarines or shipwrecks

slides.note: Ping! Echo se samundar ke raaz khulte hain.

slides.title: Sound sensors on guard
bullets: Drones and aircraft produce a characteristic low frequency humming from their motors and engines.
Even when they are hard to see, sensitive sound sensors detect this hum; the method is called audio surveillance.
Audio surveillance helps monitor airspace for safety and security.
Researchers also listen to the tiny crackles produced by microbes in the soil to study soil health and biodiversity.
slides.note: Kaan lagao, drone pakdo!

flashcards.front: What is the speed of sound?
flashcards.back: The distance which a point on a wave, such as a crest or trough, travels in unit time; that is, how fast the density disturbances move through the medium.

flashcards.front: Write the relation between speed, wavelength and frequency of a wave.
flashcards.back: Speed = wavelength / time period = wavelength x frequency. The book gives this as Equation 10.2.

flashcards.front: Rank solids, liquids and gases by speed of sound.
flashcards.back: Fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases. Sound is about 4-5 times faster in water and 15-20 times faster in solids than in air.

flashcards.front: Speed of sound in dry air at 0 degrees C and at 22 degrees C?
flashcards.back: About 331 m/s at 0 degrees C and nearly 344 m/s at 22 degrees C; the speed increases with temperature and humidity.

flashcards.front: What is pitch?
flashcards.back: Pitch is how frequency is perceived by humans. Higher frequency sounds are generally shrill with high pitch; lower frequency sounds are deep with low pitch.

flashcards.front: What is the human audible range?
flashcards.back: From 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). This range varies from person to person and decreases with age.

flashcards.front: Define infrasonic and ultrasonic waves by frequency.
flashcards.back: Infrasonic waves have frequency below 20 Hz; ultrasonic waves have frequency above 20 kHz. Humans cannot hear either.

flashcards.front: Which animals detect ultrasound and which detect infrasound?
flashcards.back: Dogs, cats, bats and dolphins can detect ultrasound, while elephants can detect infrasound.

flashcards.front: What physical property does loudness reflect?
flashcards.back: Loudness is the human perception of amplitude: larger amplitude sounds louder, and loudness decreases with distance from the source.

flashcards.front: What is reflection of sound?
flashcards.back: Sound waves bouncing off obstacles like solids or liquids is known as reflection of sound. An echo is the most common example.

flashcards.front: State the laws of reflection for sound.
flashcards.back: The incident and reflected sound make equal angles with the normal at the point of incidence, and all three directions lie in the same plane.

flashcards.front: Which phenomenon's reflection laws does sound follow?
flashcards.back: Sound follows the same laws of reflection as those of light.

flashcards.front: What is an echo?
flashcards.back: If we shout near a mountain, cliff or long corridor, the sound reflects off the hard surface of a distant object and comes back; this repeat is an echo.

flashcards.front: What minimum time gap lets us hear two sounds separately?
flashcards.back: At least 0.1 s. If the gap is less than 0.1 s, the brain cannot clearly distinguish between the sounds.

flashcards.front: Minimum distance for an echo at 340 m/s?
flashcards.back: 17 m. In 0.1 s sound covers 340 x 0.1 = 34 m to the surface and back, so the surface must be at least half of 34 m away.

flashcards.front: Why are echoes weak near curtains?
flashcards.back: Soft surfaces like curtains absorb sound, and rough surfaces scatter it in different directions, so clear echoes are not heard.

flashcards.front: What is reverberation?
flashcards.back: Multiple reflections from the walls of a large hall make sound persist after the source stops emitting it; this is reverberation.

flashcards.front: What time difference between reflections causes reverberation?
flashcards.back: Less than 0.05 s. Reflections arriving this close together make the sound persist after the source stops.

flashcards.front: How do auditoriums reduce unwanted reverberation?
flashcards.back: Using sound absorbing panels, upholstered chairs, curtains and other soft, porous surfaces so sound stays clear and undistorted.

flashcards.front: What is special about the Whispering Gallery of Gol Gumbaz?
flashcards.back: In Bijapur, Karnataka, its large dome lets even a faint whisper be heard multiple times across the dome.

flashcards.front: What are infrasonic and ultrasonic waves?
flashcards.back: Infrasonic waves have frequencies below 20 Hz and ultrasonic waves above 20 kHz; both lie outside the human audible range.

flashcards.front: What is infrasonic sound used to detect?
flashcards.back: Natural events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, and severe storms, since infrasound travels long distances through air and the Earth.

flashcards.front: What is ultrasonography?
flashcards.back: Using ultrasound to image internal organs without surgery.

flashcards.front: List industrial uses of ultrasonic waves.
flashcards.back: Ultrasonic welding, cleaning delicate machine parts, and detecting defects inside metal blocks during construction and industrial testing.

flashcards.front: What is echolocation?
flashcards.back: The ability to locate objects using reflected sound waves. Bats emit ultrasonic bursts and sense the echoes to find obstacles and prey.

flashcards.front: Which animals use echolocation besides bats?
flashcards.back: Dolphins, whales and some birds also use echolocation for navigation and hunting.

flashcards.front: What is sonar and what does it measure?
flashcards.back: Sound navigation and ranging: ultrasonic waves sent into water and their reflections reveal the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects.

flashcards.front: What is audio surveillance?
flashcards.back: Detecting the low frequency humming of drones and aircraft using sensitive sound sensors, to monitor airspace for safety and security.

quiz.q: In which type of medium does sound travel fastest?
options: It travels equally fast in all media
quiz.why: The book says sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

quiz.q: Compared to air, sound in water travels about:
quiz.why: The book gives about 4-5 times faster in water and 15-20 times faster in solids.

quiz.q: The speed of sound in dry air is about 331 m/s at 0 degrees C. What is it nearly at 22 degrees C?
quiz.why: Speed increases with temperature: nearly 344 m/s at 22 degrees C in dry air.

quiz.q: A sound of frequency 20 kHz travels in air at 344 m/s. Its wavelength is about:
quiz.why: Wavelength = speed / frequency = 344 / 20000 = 0.0172 m = 1.72 cm, from Example 10.2.

quiz.q: How do humans perceive the frequency of a sound?
quiz.why: Pitch is how frequency is perceived by humans, while amplitude is perceived as loudness.

quiz.q: A thunder rumble sounds deep. Its pitch is:
quiz.why: Deep sounds like thunder or an aircraft rumble have low pitch and lower frequency.

quiz.q: The human audible range is:
quiz.why: The audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz; it varies from person to person and decreases with age.

quiz.q: Why do boys' voices usually deepen during adolescence?
options: Vocal cords lengthen and thicken, vibrating less frequently
Vocal cords shorten and vibrate more often
The mouth stops shaping the sound
quiz.why: During adolescence, boys' vocal cords lengthen and thicken and vibrate less frequently, deepening the voice.

quiz.q: As you walk farther from a street musician, the loudness of the music:
quiz.why: The book states loudness decreases as we move farther away from the source.

quiz.q: In Activity 10.8, students lower a tone from 50 Hz until it just becomes inaudible. That happens near:
quiz.why: Hearing stops around 20 Hz, the lower edge of the human audible range.

quiz.q: Sound follows the same laws of reflection as:
quiz.why: The book says sound follows the same laws of reflection as those of light.

quiz.q: A sound wave strikes a wall at 40 degrees to the normal. The reflected sound leaves at:
quiz.why: Incident and reflected sound make equal angles with the normal at the point of incidence.

quiz.q: The incident sound, the normal and the reflected sound always:
options: Leave at right angles to each other
quiz.why: Like light, all three directions lie in the same plane during reflection of sound.

quiz.q: You shout near a cliff and hear your voice again. This repeated sound is called:
quiz.why: The sound reflects off the hard surface of a distant object and comes back as an echo.

quiz.q: Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the minimum distance of a surface for hearing a distinct echo is:
quiz.why: In 0.1 s sound covers 34 m to the surface and back, so the surface must be at least 17 m away.

quiz.q: You clap in an empty corridor and hear an echo after 0.5 s (speed 340 m/s). Your distance from the wall is:
quiz.why: The sound goes to the wall and back: distance = 340 x 0.5, halved to 85 m, as in Example 10.5.

quiz.q: Why can you not hear an echo of your voice in a small room?
options: Walls completely absorb every sound wave
Reflections arrive too quickly for the brain to separate them
quiz.why: Wall reflections arrive with a gap below 0.1 s, so they blend with the original sound.

quiz.q: An experiment needs echoes at least 0.2 s after emission. With sound speed 343 m/s, the surface should be at least:
quiz.why: Round trip = 343 x 0.2 = 68.6 m, so minimum one-way distance = 34.3 m (Pause and Ponder 12).

quiz.q: In a large hall, sound persisting after the singer stops is called:
quiz.why: Multiple reflections from the walls make sound persist after the source stops; this is reverberation.

quiz.q: Reverberation occurs when sound reflections arrive with a time difference of:
quiz.why: The book states reverberation occurs when reflections arrive with a time difference less than 0.05 s.

quiz.q: Which materials help reduce unwanted reverberation in an auditorium?
options: Sound absorbing panels, upholstered chairs and curtains
Polished granite walls and a glass roof
quiz.why: Soft, porous surfaces absorb sound; hard, smooth ones would add reflections and garble it.

quiz.q: Sound waves with frequency below 20 Hz are called:
quiz.why: Below 20 Hz is infrasonic; above 20 kHz is ultrasonic; both are outside human hearing.

quiz.q: Ultrasonography is used by doctors to:
quiz.why: The book lists ultrasonography as imaging internal organs without surgery using ultrasound.

quiz.q: Infrasonic waves are especially useful for detecting:
options: Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and severe storms
quiz.why: Infrasound travels long distances through air and the Earth, so it detects natural events and storms.

quiz.q: Which of these is a use of ultrasonic, not infrasonic, waves?
options: Detecting severe storms across long distances
Detecting defects inside metal blocks in industrial testing
quiz.why: Detecting defects inside metal blocks is listed among the ultrasound applications in the book.

quiz.q: Bats fly and hunt in the dark using short bursts of:
quiz.why: Most bats emit short bursts of ultrasonic waves which are reflected from nearby objects.

quiz.q: Sonar stands for:
quiz.why: Sonar means sound navigation and ranging, adapted from echolocation for underwater exploration.

quiz.q: A naval sonar signal returns after 0.90 s. Speed of sound in seawater is 1530 m/s. How far is the object?
quiz.why: One-way time is 0.90 / 2 = 0.45 s, so distance = 1530 x 0.45 = 688.5 m (Example 10.6).

quiz.q: A sonar signal sent to find ocean depth returns after 4 s. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in seawater, the depth is:
quiz.why: One-way time is 2 s, so depth = 1500 x 2 = 3000 m (Pause and Ponder 13).

quiz.q: Audio surveillance spots hard-to-see drones and aircraft by detecting:
options: The low frequency humming of their motors and engines
quiz.why: Sensitive sound sensors pick up the characteristic low frequency humming to monitor airspace.

examples.title: Hearing range in wavelengths
examples.problem: Human hearing roughly spans 20 Hz to 20 kHz. What are the corresponding wavelengths in air? Use the speed of sound in air as 344 m/s. (Book Example 10.2)
steps: Use the wave relation: speed of the wave = frequency x wavelength, so wavelength = speed / frequency.
Notice the span: the longest wavelength we hear is about 1000 times longer than the shortest.
examples.answer: The wavelength is 17.2 m for 20 Hz and 1.72 cm for 20000 Hz.

examples.title: How far is that lightning?
examples.problem: During a thunderstorm, the flash of lightning is seen and the thunder is heard 5 s later. Light travels at 300000 km/s, reaching you almost instantaneously. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, estimate the distance to the lightning strike. (Book Example 10.3)
steps: Light is so fast that the flash reaches you almost instantaneously; the whole 5 s delay is the sound's travel time.
Use the relation: distance = speed x time.
This is why sound's slow speed makes thunder always trail the lightning flash.
examples.answer: The lightning strike is about 1700 m away.

examples.title: Echo off a corridor wall
examples.problem: You clap in an empty corridor and hear an echo after 0.5 s. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, calculate your distance from the wall. (Book Example 10.5)
steps: The sound travels to the wall and comes back, so the wall is at half the total path length.
Total distance travelled = speed x time = 340 m/s x 0.5 s = 170 m.
Check: 85 m is well beyond the 17 m minimum echo distance, so a distinct echo is possible.
examples.answer: You are standing 85 m from the wall.

examples.title: Sonar finds a hidden object
examples.problem: A naval sonar signal sent into seawater returns after 0.90 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1530 m/s. How far is the object? (Book Example 10.6)
steps: The 0.90 s is the round-trip time: the signal goes to the object and comes back.
Time taken to reach the object = 0.90 / 2 = 0.45 s.
Distance = speed x time = 1530 m/s x 0.45 s = 688.5 m.
